title: Constructible etale biduality over a complete strictly henselian trait
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime and $A=\mathbf F_\ell$. Let $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, where $R$ is a complete strictly henselian discrete valuation ring of mixed characteristic on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Completeness is for the maximal-ideal topology; mixed characteristic means that the fraction field has characteristic zero and the residue field has positive characteristic. Let $p:X\to S$ be finite type and quasi-projective [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], meaning that $X$ admits a locally closed immersion into $\mathbf P^n_S$ for some finite $n$. Use ordinary small-etale derived categories of constant-$A$ module sheaves [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories]. Let $p^!$ be the ambient right adjoint to ordinary compact-support direct image and put $Q_X=p^!A_S$ [thm-amb-etale-exceptional-adjoint]. Then $Q_X$ is bounded constructible [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes], and $D_X(M)=R\mathcal Hom_A(M,Q_X)$ [def-pur-derived-internal-hom] preserves $D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{et}},A)$. For every $M\in D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{et}},A)$ the canonical map
$$\eta_M:M\longrightarrow D_XD_XM,$$
obtained by transposing evaluation $D_XM\otimes_A^L M\to Q_X$ after symmetry [def-kun-derived-tensor], is an isomorphism, naturally in $M$. No regularity or punctual-purity hypothesis on $X$ is imposed.

source.place: Expose XVI, proof of Lemma 3.5.9, printed p.250: the local biduality theorem invoked for the relative dualizing complex. This node isolates that general constructible biduality input, with the complete mixed-characteristic trait hypotheses of section 3.7, rather than the scalar-endomorphism consequence.

proof.text: The DVR $R$ is Noetherian because every ideal is principal. Completeness gives excellence. It is regular: its only primes are $(0)$ and its maximal ideal, and their local rings are a field and a one-dimensional local ring with principal maximal ideal. Finite-type affine charts of $X$ are Noetherian and excellent. Apply the independent trait lemma to $S$: $A_S$ is dualizing. Unlike the rejected smooth-pullback input, that lemma uses only the dimension-one tame-inertia calculation.

source.place: XVII sections 1.2.1–1.2.3; Stacks Tag 07QW for excellence

proof.text:
We prove an auxiliary assertion within this proof by induction. Fields are excellent; the products are Noetherian excellent by finite-type stability. Each projective-line projection is proper, and their composites are proper. For a field $T=\operatorname{Spec}k$ with $\ell$ invertible, or an excellent strictly henselian DVR trait $T$, put $W_n(T)=(\mathbf P^1_T)^n$ and $\pi_n:W_n(T)\to T$. Composing the normalized projective-line adjunctions gives
$$\Omega_{n,T}=\pi_n^\times A_T\cong A_{W_n(T)}(n)[2n].$$
Here twists are the ordinary etale roots-of-unity rank-one sheaves. At $n=0$ this is the identity adjunction. The base-change clause of the projective-line adjunction and pullback of twists give these identifications after every regular base change used below. Internal Hom into $\Omega_{n,T}$ preserves $D^b_c$ by the low-base Hom-finiteness lemma; the target is bounded constructible since its twist is locally free of rank one. Thus for every $M\in D^b_c$ the cone $C_M$ of its specified evaluation bidual map is bounded constructible, before any biduality is assumed.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, printed p.298: constructible cone; here use actual projective-line adjoints and low-base finiteness

proof.text:
For a proper projection $r:W_n(T)\to T$, internal adjunction gives
$$a_M:Rr_*D_WM\xrightarrow{\sim}D_TRr_*M,$$
where $D_T=R\mathcal Hom_A(-,A_T)$. Both $M$ and $D_WM$ are bounded constructible by the preceding step, and their proper images are bounded constructible. Applying $a$ again gives
$$b_M=D_T(a_M^{-1})a_{D_WM}:Rr_*D_W^2M\xrightarrow{\sim}D_T^2Rr_*M.$$
It satisfies $b_M Rr_*\eta_M=\eta_{Rr_*M}$. Indeed transpose both maps against $D_TRr_*M$, precompose this factor by $a_M$, and use the evaluation normalization of internal adjunction. Both transposes become the direct-image tensor map followed by $Rr_*$ of evaluation after symmetry and the exceptional counit $Rr_*\Omega_{n,T}\to A_T$. Naturality of evaluation cancels $a_M^{-1}a_M$, so the transposes and hence the maps agree. This argument uses no potential complexes or biduality on $W_n(T)$.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, last paragraph: proper comparison, derived here directly from internal adjunction

proof.text: Under any regular base change $g:T'\to T$ between the fields or excellent traits occurring below, and also under a strict localization of a coordinate projective line, the pullback of $\Omega_{n,T}$ is the displayed twist-shift for the corresponding product, up to a common invertible twist-shift if we regard one coordinate as part of the new base. Regular base change of internal Hom applies first to $M$ and then to $D_WM$, since step 2 proves both bounded constructible. The resulting comparison identifies the pullback of $\eta_M$ with evaluation biduality on the new product. Common invertible twist-shifts cancel by the twisted-bidual transport lemma. In particular $C_M$ pulls back to its biduality cone there. Strict localizations are Noetherian excellent and regular as morphisms, as stipulated in the internal-Hom comparison lemma.

source.place: XVII Proposition 4.2.2 and Proposition 6.4.2 proof, localization argument; no pinning clause used

proof.text: First prove biduality on $W_n(k)$ simultaneously for every field $k$ of characteristic different from $\ell$, by induction on $n$. At $n=0$, a constructible sheaf on $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a finite-dimensional continuous Galois representation. After a finite separable cover it is a finite free constant sheaf, so internal Hom is its ordinary linear dual; evaluation into the double dual is the ordinary finite-dimensional isomorphism. For bounded complexes the result follows from cohomological truncations and the triangle property of evaluation. For the inductive step one may replace $k$ by a separable closure: this is the strict localization of the field, so the regular-comparison lemma applies and its pullback tests every geometric stalk, and step 4 identifies the biduality map after this change. Hence it suffices to treat separably closed $k$.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, dimension-zero induction; finite-dimensional evaluation base case

proof.text: Let $n>0$ and $M\in D^b_c(W_n(k),A)$, with $k$ separably closed. For each coordinate projection $r_j:W_n(k)\to\mathbf P^1_k$, pull back to a geometric generic point of $\mathbf P^1_k$. This is the strict localization at its generic point, hence regular by the cited strict-localization statement. The resulting scheme is $W_{n-1}(k(t)^{\mathrm{sep}})$. Step 4 identifies the cone there, including the cancelled common twist-shift, and the induction hypothesis on $n$ says it vanishes. Thus if $C_{M,z}\ne0$, every coordinate image of $z$ is nongeneric in $\mathbf P^1_k$, hence closed. The closed-points-of-product lemma, iterated, implies that $z$ is closed in $W_n(k)$. Therefore all cohomology of $C_M$ is supported at closed points.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, coordinate-projection argument, specialized to dimension zero

proof.text: Apply step 3 to $\pi_n:W_n(k)\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Since the field base has biduality by step 5 and $R\pi_{n,*}M$ is bounded constructible, step 3 shows $R\pi_{n,*}C_M=0$. The closed-support detection lemma over a separably closed field applies to $C_M$, whose support was just shown to consist of closed points. It gives $C_M=0$. This proves the induction for all fields. This argument includes $M=0$, $n=0$, and imperfect separably closed ground fields; no claim that such a field is perfect is used.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, final cone-detection argument; Stacks Tag 0F1G

proof.text: Next prove the assertion for $W_n(T)$ simultaneously for all excellent strictly henselian DVR traits $T$ with $\ell$ invertible, again by induction on $n$. The case $n=0$ is the independent trait lemma, which needs neither completeness nor mixed characteristic. Let $n>0$. Restriction to the generic field of $T$ is regular. Step 4 and the field result show that the cone $C_M$ is zero outside the closed fibre $W_n(s)$, where $s$ is the separably closed residue field. This establishes the support reduction without a closed-fibre purity or costalk comparison.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, outer dimension induction, restricted to traits

proof.text: Let $y$ be the generic point of $\mathbf P^1_s\subset\mathbf P^1_T$ and choose a geometric point over $y$. Put $T'=(\mathbf P^1_T)_{(\bar y)}$. The special fibre is integral and Cartier: on either affine chart it is defined by the nonzerodivisor uniformizer of $T$, with quotient $\kappa(s)[t]$. These charts are regular by polynomial regularity over the regular DVR. Thus the generic Cartier stalk lemma makes $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_T,y}$ a DVR, and strict henselization preserves this property. The strict localization lemma gives excellence of $T'$ and regularity of its map to $\mathbf P^1_T$. Hence $T'$ is another excellent strictly henselian DVR trait with $\ell$ invertible. It need not be complete; this is why the trait input has been stated without completeness.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, scheme Y at the generic point of the coordinate special fibre; generic Cartier/DVR geometry

proof.text: For each of the $n$ coordinate projections $r_j:W_n(T)\to\mathbf P^1_T$, the base change along $T'\to\mathbf P^1_T$ is $W_{n-1}(T')$. By step 4 its cone is the pullback of $C_M$: $\Omega_{n,T}$ pulls back to $A(n)[2n]$, differing from $\Omega_{n-1,T'}$ only by the invertible factor $A(1)[2]$. The induction hypothesis on $n$, applied to this new trait $T'$, kills the pullback. A nonzero stalk at a point above the generic point $y$ would remain nonzero at some point of this surjective geometric extension, so $C_{M,z}\ne0$ implies that the image of $z$ under $r_j$ is not $y$. Step 8 already places $z$ in the closed fibre. All its coordinate images in $\mathbf P^1_s$ are therefore closed. The product lemma again makes $z$ a closed point of $W_n(s)$.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, inner induction on projective-line factors at the generic special-fibre point

proof.text: Proper comparison in step 3, the trait base case, and proper constructible preservation give $R\pi_{n,*}C_M=0$. Since $C_M$ restricts to zero off $W_n(s)$, open/closed recollement identifies it with $i_*i^*C_M$ for $i:W_n(s)\hookrightarrow W_n(T)$. Proper base change at $s$ identifies $s^*R\pi_{n,*}C_M$ with $R\Gamma(W_n(s),i^*C_M)$; it is zero. The residue field is separably closed, and step 10 proved that $i^*C_M$ is supported at closed points. Stacks Tag 0F1G therefore gives $i^*C_M=0$, whence $C_M=0$. This completes both inductions and proves bounded constructible biduality on every product $W_n(T)$ used here.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, proper-image and closed-support detection

proof.text: Fix an affine chart $U=\operatorname{Spec}B$ of $X$. Finitely many algebra generators give a closed immersion $i:U\hookrightarrow V=\mathbf A^m_S$. Regard $V$ as the product of the standard affine opens in $W_m(S)$; the affine-space open-immersion lemma is used with $n=1$ in each factor. Write $j:V\hookrightarrow W_m(S)$ and $q:V\to S$. Open locality identifies $K=q^\times A_S$ with $j^*\Omega_{m,S}$. For any $M\in D^b_c(V,A)$, $j_!M$ is bounded constructible: exactness gives the same cohomological bounds; extend the finite constructible stratification of each cohomology sheaf by the closed complement with value zero, using the inside/outside stalk formula. All strata remain locally closed constructible since the ambient scheme is Noetherian. Moreover $j^*j_!M=M$ by that stalk formula. Restrict the biduality of $j_!M$ from step 11. Restriction of internal Hom respects evaluation and tensor symmetry, hence gives the specified biduality for $M$ with target $K$. The same restriction gives bounded constructibility of $K$ and of $R\mathcal Hom_A(M,K)$. This proves the ambient-chart input.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, initial affine embedding reduction, applied after the product induction

proof.text: With $K=q^\times A_S$ from step 12, put $Q_U=i^!K$. The finite-adjunction lemma identifies this bounded-below right adjoint with the restriction of the ambient adjoint; in particular $i^!K\in D^+(U,A)$. Compact-support composition and uniqueness of right adjoints identify $i^!q^\times A_S$ with $(p|_U)^\times A_S$. Open locality identifies the latter with $Q_X|_U$. All these comparisons are the counit-compatible adjunction comparisons. Since $i$ is closed, it is finite, with $Ri_!=i_*$, so there is no regular-immersion requirement at this step.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, affine closed-support reduction; explicit finite-adjunction descent and gluing

proof.text:
For $M\in D^b_c(U,A)$, exact finite direct image makes $i_*M$ bounded constructible on $V$. The finite internal-adjunction isomorphism gives
$$a_M:i_*R\mathcal Hom_A(M,Q_U)\xrightarrow{\sim}D_V(i_*M).$$
The right-hand side is bounded constructible by step 12. Closed geometric stalks identify the stalks of $i_*F$ on $i(U)$ with those of $F$. Hence the counit $i^*i_*F\to F$ is an isomorphism, as can be tested on these stalks. Exact inverse image and constructible pullback therefore show that $D_UM=R\mathcal Hom_A(M,Q_U)\cong i^*D_V(i_*M)$ is bounded constructible. Apply this with $M=A_U$: on each etale object, an $A$-linear map from the free rank-one module $A$ is determined by its value at $1$, so $R\mathcal Hom_A(A_U,Q_U)=Q_U$. Thus $Q_U$ itself is bounded constructible. This proves boundedness before taking any second dual.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, affine closed-support reduction; explicit finite-adjunction descent and gluing

proof.text:
We check the specified map, not merely existence of an abstract double-dual isomorphism. Apply the same $a$ to $D_UM$, which step 14 has proved bounded constructible. There is an isomorphism
$$b_M=D_V(a_M^{-1})\circ a_{D_UM}:i_*D_U^2M\xrightarrow{\sim}D_V^2(i_*M).$$
The normalization in finite internal adjunction sends evaluation on $U$ to the pairing on $V$ obtained by first evaluating and then applying the counit $i_*Q_U\to K$. To see the iteration compatibility, pair both $b_M i_*\eta^U_M$ and $\eta^V_{i_*M}$ with $D_V(i_*M)$ and precompose that factor by $a_M$. For each expression, tensor--Hom adjunction cancels the transpose, and naturality of evaluation cancels $a_M^{-1}a_M$. The resulting pairing is in both cases
$$i_*M\otimes i_*D_UM\longrightarrow i_*(M\otimes D_UM)\xrightarrow{i_*(\mathrm{ev}\circ\mathrm{sym})}i_*Q_U\longrightarrow K.$$
Thus adjunction gives $b_M i_*\eta^U_M=\eta^V_{i_*M}$. The last map is invertible by step 12, so $i_*\eta^U_M$ is invertible. Exactness of $i_*$ and its closed-stalk formula show that its cone vanishes if and only if the original cone vanishes. Hence $\eta^U_M$ is invertible, naturally in $M$.

source.place: XVII Proposition 6.4.2 proof, affine closed-support reduction; explicit finite-adjunction descent and gluing

proof.text: For $M\in D^b_c(X,A)$, slice restriction commutes with derived internal Hom. Together with step 13 this identifies $(D_XM)|_{U_a}$ with $D_{U_a}(M|_{U_a})$, and a second application identifies $(D_X^2M)|_{U_a}$ with $D_{U_a}^2(M|_{U_a})$. The comparisons respect evaluation and tensor symmetry, so they identify the restriction of $\eta_M$ with the map proved invertible in step 15. Each $Q_X|_{U_a}$ and $(D_XM)|_{U_a}$ is bounded constructible. Since the affine cover is finite, the union of their finitely many cohomological intervals is bounded; constructibility is local on this cover by its finite-stratification definition. Hence $Q_X,D_XM\in D^b_c(X,A)$. The cone of $\eta_M$ restricts to zero on the cover, so each of its geometric stalks is zero, and therefore each cohomology sheaf is zero. Thus $\eta_M$ is an isomorphism. All comparisons are natural in $M$, and the symmetry-transposed evaluation defines a natural transformation for arbitrary dualizing target, so the resulting isomorphism is natural. No step assumes regularity or punctual purity of $X$.
